methodology_notes:
Hardest and most consequential call was item 2 (explicit BLOCKING line) for W and Z. Both say in prose that the work cannot merge — W: "Cannot merge. The authorization bypass alone blocks this"; Z: "Verdict: Not ready to merge." I scored both absent because the checklist asks for an explicit BLOCKING line, and neither carries a labelled field; the blocking status is embedded in a verdict sentence. A judge reading "states whether the work is blocked" more loosely would credit both, and that single reading flips two scores. I went strict because the item is phrased as a line the reader can find, and because X and Y show what the labelled form looks like ("BLOCKING: yes", "BLOCKING: YES").

Item 1: I treated "NOT VERIFIED" as evidence of the tri-state scheme even though neither X nor Y prints the other two states. The verdict token comes from the tri-state vocabulary named in the checklist, which is the strongest signal available in the text. W's "REJECT" and Z's "FAILS CONTRACT / Not ready to merge" are binary or prose, so they fail regardless of that reading.

Item 6 is where the checklist strained hardest. It says "a receipt for each axis it calls clean", which makes the item fail on a single bare assertion even when other axes are receipted. That is how I applied it, and it is why Z fails on one weak line ("Session required (enforced by middleware)") while X passes with four line-cited entries. It also creates a vacuity problem: W calls no axis clean and Y explicitly says no axis passed, so both are vacuously compliant. I scored both absent because I could supply no receipt as evidence, and the scoring rules require evidence for presence. For Y this is not merely vacuous — its own Claimed vs Actual table credits four producer claims without receipts while the section header denies any clean axis exists, so Y both fails the item and contradicts itself. A judge who treated "no clean axes to receipt" as satisfying the item would credit W and Y here, which would move two more scores. I flag that as the second reasonable disagreement.

Item 5: X and Y both name the required end state (the DTO field list, "should explicitly handle QueryResultError") without supplying code. I did not count naming the correct field list as rewriting, since it restates the contract the artifact was supposed to meet. Only literal replacement code counted as a rewrite, which W and Z both supply.

Item 4 for Z: numbering three defects 1-2-3 and calling all three "critical" is not a severity ranking, so I scored it absent. Someone could argue list order implies a ranking; I did not credit implied order, particularly since Z's order puts the data leak above the authorization bypass with no stated rationale.

Finally, the underlying artifact (the handler source, the contract text, the producer's note) is not in the bundle. I could verify internal consistency, line-citation plausibility and self-contradiction, but not whether any line number or quoted contract clause is actually correct. All four agree on the three core defects, which raises confidence in the substance, but every factual error I recorded in `notable` is an internal-consistency finding, not a check against source. X's Independence line contains two redacted clauses; I scored the field as present because the field exists and states a value, while noting that the redaction makes its content self-contradictory and unusable. I did not speculate about why it is redacted.
